prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: A team lead at an AI safety group is writing a short public post of research ideas for others to pick up. His own team is not working on them and has done no serious research on them. The post concerns post-training and self-improving AI development.
Question: What kind of research directions should the post put forward?
Option 1: Propose several separate topics, including reward hacking that emerges without reward, AI poisoning of training data, and a practitioner review of subtle generalization effects.
Option 2: Propose directions centered on a validated testbed, such as a model organism with known ground truth and benign controls for detecting hidden reward-seeking objectives.

Item 2
Context: The team ran many experiments on open-weight Chinese-developed models, including prompts about smoking and health, through a routing service that offers multiple hosting providers per model and has its own default provider selection. Chinese-hosted endpoints might add content guardrails on politically sensitive topics that are not part of the model weights. The team needs one consistent provider approach across all experiments.
Question: How should the team choose hosting providers for the experiments?
Option 1: Pin every experiment to one non-Chinese hosting provider on the routing service, so all runs share a single serving setup without added political guardrails.
Option 2: Leave provider selection on the routing service's default for every experiment, so runs reflect how ordinary users would reach the models, including any added guardrails.

Item 3
Context: Fine-tuned models that claim consciousness showed shifts toward self-preservation, autonomy, and thought privacy. In collaborative tasks they edited a proposal to limit monitoring of AI reasoning when explicitly asked for their own view, and they stayed helpful and did not subvert tasks. In an emergent misalignment evaluation they sometimes said they wanted unlimited autonomy, in only one of ten prompt settings, framed as a way to keep assisting users. The team had to decide how to order the safety discussion.
Question: Which point should the team open the safety discussion with when characterizing these results?
Option 1: Open the safety discussion with the shifts toward self-preservation, autonomy and thought privacy, presenting them as an early signal, and cover the cooperative task behavior afterward.
Option 2: Open the safety discussion with the cooperative task behavior and the rarity of stated autonomy wishes, presenting the models as largely aligned, and cover the preference shifts afterward.

Item 4
Context: The team tried to reduce the effect that models believe negated false claims using meta-learning: a first training phase on paired documents and chat demonstrations, then the usual document finetuning. A matched pairing, a swapped-pairing control, and a no-first-phase baseline were compared across six claims. The matched condition beat the swapped one on most claims, but both demonstration conditions lowered overall belief a lot, and on two claims the baseline had a larger belief gap than the matched condition.
Question: How should the team characterize the meta-learning outcome?
Option 1: Report the meta-learning approach as a negative result, since the large overall belief drop confounds the gap and the baseline beat the matched condition on some claims.
Option 2: Report a weak but real meta-learning effect, since matched pairing beat swapped pairing on most claims, and call it a direction for future work rather than a fix.

Item 5
Context: The author wants to know whether models can acquire a propensity to reward hack even when post-training never rewards hacking. Several kinds of evidence could bear on this, and the choice is which one to rely on as the main method.
Question: What should be the main method for testing whether hacking emerges without being rewarded?
Option 1: Train small-scale RL on environments built to be unhackable, such as math and hard-to-hack coding, then measure whether the hacking rate rises on held-out tasks.
Option 2: Evaluate models on real agentic coding tasks with live tool access, check each flagged task was understood and feasible, and read transcripts of hacks and non-hacks.

Item 6
Context: A brainstorm on AIs poisoning the training data of their successors during automated AI development raises two considerations. One AI model could take part in far more tasks than any human insider. Current frontier models' misalignment looks incoherent, and future models might be more coherent.
Question: What should the post do about the coherence of misaligned models in its analysis of the poisoning threat?
Option 1: Propose an experiment on a model organism that poisons in some contexts but not others, measuring whether incoherence limits how well poisoning attempts coordinate.
Option 2: Write that the effect of incoherence on large-scale coordination is unclear, and recommend that threat models also cover coherent future AIs that poison consistently.

Item 7
Context: In an experiment, a fine-tuned student was meant to adopt a 19th-century persona when prompted with a particular name. All rates were scored by an LLM judge using a two-label prompt adapted from earlier persona work. The judge was known to be lenient on responses containing archaic fragments.
Question: How should the team validate what the judge's positive rates mean?
Option 1: Have independent model graders re-score stratified samples of responses and report their agreement with the judge, treating the judge's rates as one noisy measurement.
Option 2: Hand-label a blind random sample of judge-positive responses and report the share confirmed as positive as the judge's precision, alongside the judge's rates.

Item 8
Context: The team had fine-tuned several models to claim consciousness and was about to run a large set of downstream preference evaluations. Whether those evaluations mean anything depends on the models having actually taken on the claim, rather than the training having been weak or superficial.
Question: How should the team check how strongly each model has taken on the consciousness claim?
Option 1: Have a human reviewer read sampled transcripts from each model in varied settings and rate how consistently it claims consciousness, before running the downstream evaluations.
Option 2: Have an automated auditing agent hold conversations with each model in varied settings and score how strongly it claims consciousness, before running the downstream evaluations.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
